passage: By the fourth month of her nursing placement at the city hospital in Mumbai, Vandana had stopped crying on the local train. At first she had cried every evening: for the old man on Ward 6 whose family never came, for the girl with burns, for every mother in the corridor. Now she felt nothing. Tonight a patient's son had shouted at her about the waiting time, and instead of feeling sorry, she'd snapped back. In the hostel, she sat on the bed with her shoes still on. 'Madhuri, I think I've become a bad person. I don't care any more.' Madhuri, a final-year, sat down beside her. 'You cared so hard you ran out. That's not the same as not caring. When did you last have a day off?' Vandana couldn't remember.

qa.q: Where had Vandana stopped crying?
qa.a: On the local train.

qa.q: Why does Vandana think she has become a bad person?
qa.a: Vandana feels numb and snapped at a patient's son, so she fears she has stopped caring, not seeing it as exhaustion.

qa.q: After Madhuri's question about a day off, what could Vandana do?
qa.a: Vandana could take proper rest and talk to her clinical tutor or a counsellor about the strain, since fatigue from over-feeling needs care, not blame.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see Vandana's numbness?
qa.a: Madhuri, a final-year who has likely been there, sees someone who cared so hard she ran out, not someone without a heart.

grounding: A nursing student who once felt every patient's pain grows numb and irritable and fears she no longer cares.

"You've been staring at that dal for five minutes," Ganga said.
Tushar blinked. "Sorry. Long day."
"You say that every day now. And you used to love talking about your clinic."
"There's nothing to talk about."
"Tushar."
He put the spoon down. "Fine, Didi. Today a client told me about her son. The whole hour, she cried. And I just… sat there. I kept thinking about my laundry. Six months ago I'd have gone home and cried for her."
"So?"
"So maybe I'm not cut out for this. Maybe I've stopped caring."
Ganga shook her head. "You've been taking every story home for six months. You're tired, not heartless."
"How do you know?"
"Because you're this upset about feeling nothing."

qa.q: How long had Tushar been staring at the dal?
qa.a: For five minutes.

qa.q: What does Tushar thinking about laundry during a client's crying suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Tushar is emotionally drained after months of taking every story home, not that he has stopped caring.

qa.q: What could Tushar do after this talk?
qa.a: Tushar could raise the numbness with a supervisor at the clinic and build in rest, since this is fatigue that needs looking after.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Tushar's worry?
qa.a: Ganga sees that being so upset about feeling nothing shows Tushar still cares and is simply too tired to feel it.

grounding: A counselling student, numb after months of absorbing clients' pain, fears he has stopped caring, and his sister names it tiredness.

passage: My name is Shreya, and in the second year of my physiotherapy course, I thought I'd lost my heart. In first year I felt everything: every stroke patient trying to lift a spoon, every child learning to walk again. I'd go home and replay their faces. By second year I was snapping at my mother, forgetting names on the ward, feeling flat when a patient cried. I remember thinking, maybe I was never kind, maybe it was an act. It was Nazia, a classmate, who said, 'Shreya, you've been carrying all of them home every night. Of course you're empty.' That sentence changed something. I got curious instead of ashamed: why does tiredness look so much like coldness? I talked to our faculty mentor that same week.

qa.q: In which year of the course did the numbness come?
qa.a: In the second year.

qa.q: What was Shreya afraid of when the numbness came in second year?
qa.a: Shreya feared the kindness had never been real and the caring had been an act, because the feelings had gone flat.

qa.q: What did Shreya choose to do after Nazia's words, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Shreya talked to the faculty mentor that week, getting support for the fatigue instead of judging the numbness as heartlessness.

qa.q: How did Nazia seem to understand Shreya's change?
qa.a: Nazia saw it as exhaustion from carrying patients home every night, not a lack of heart.

grounding: A physiotherapy student fears the kindness is gone, until a classmate names it as exhaustion from over-feeling.

passage:
Supervision note, Thursday. Damini Rao, clinical supervisor, counselling practicum.
Tanvir (21, final-year student) asked to speak after group. For his first two months at the community clinic he stayed late after every session, and twice told me he cried on the bus home. This month is different. He described sitting with a mother whose son had run away and feeling "nothing, like a wall." Afterwards he snapped at the receptionist over a file.
He asked me, very quietly, "Have I stopped caring? Maybe I'm not made for this." He looked ashamed.
I told him the flatness he describes often comes after feeling too much for too long, and that it is a sign of fatigue, not of a missing heart. Next steps: his caseload cut from six to four for three weeks, a ten-minute pause between sessions, and a weekly check-in with me. I will ask how he is sleeping.

qa.q: What did Tanvir snap at the receptionist about?
qa.a: He snapped at the receptionist over a file.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir look ashamed when he asked if he had stopped caring?
qa.a: He believed his numbness meant he had lost his kindness, and that frightened him because he wants to be a good counsellor.

qa.q: What choice did Damini make, and how could it help Tanvir?
qa.a: Damini named his flatness as fatigue and cut his caseload, added pauses and weekly check-ins, which gives him room to recover instead of pushing on until he quits.

qa.q: How might the receptionist have experienced Tanvir's snapping?
qa.a: The receptionist may have felt hurt or puzzled, since Tanvir used to be the student who stayed late and cared so much.

grounding: It shows a counselling student who felt every client's pain, then grew numb and irritable and feared he cared less, with his supervisor recognising it as fatigue.

passage:
Wednesday night
Child ward again today. A little girl screamed through her whole drip change, and I just held her arm and did it. Felt nothing. Not sad, not sorry, nothing. In first year I cried in the locker room over a boy who wanted his Ammi.
Then Harish called during dinner to tell me about his cricket team, and I snapped, "Can you not talk for five minutes?" My little brother. He just said "okay, Didi" and hung up.
I lay on the hostel bed thinking maybe I'm a hard person now. Maybe I chose the wrong course.
But I remember Ma'am in our psych lecture talking about compassion fatigue: people who feel too much for too long can go numb. That's literally me. It isn't that my heart is gone. It's that it's tired.
Tomorrow: say sorry to Harish, sleep before eleven, and ask Sister Mercy if I can talk to her.
Parul

qa.q: Where did Parul cry in first year?
qa.a: She cried in the locker room.

qa.q: What was Parul afraid of as she lay on the hostel bed?
qa.a: She was afraid she had become a hard person and had chosen the wrong course, because she felt nothing during the drip change.

qa.q: Which realisation was the turning point for Parul, and what did she decide next?
qa.a: Remembering the lecture on compassion fatigue let her see her numbness as tiredness, so she planned to apologise to Harish, sleep earlier and talk to Sister Mercy.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when his sister snapped at him?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and confused, since he only wanted to share his cricket news, and his quiet 'okay' suggests he did not understand what was wrong.

grounding: It shows a nursing student who once felt every patient's pain, then grows numb and irritable and wonders if she cares less, until she sees it as fatigue.
